survey: Cartoon three-masted sailing ship in 3/4 side view, bow to the left, riding on waves. Hull: one wooden hull with a high curved prow on the left and a raised stern deck with railing on the right. Three gold-rimmed portholes face the camera; E1 measures 0.95 wide-to-tall and fits a true ellipse within 1.9%, so they read as round. Masts: the foremast, mainmast and mizzen each stand behind the bulwark rail and rise out of the deck. The mainmast has a collar where it goes through the deck. Each mast has one yard and a ball cap on top. Each top flies a pennant, and all three point the same way. Sails: three sails, one hanging from each yard and bellied by the wind. The mainsail sits in front of the other two; it overlaps them, but nothing passes through anything. Rigging: rope bundles at each masthead run as lifts to both yard ends, so every end attaches. Rope lashings hold each sail to its yard. The lower ropes (sheets) run from the sail bottoms down to the deck rail, or to a deck fitting at the stern. Two of these cross near the stern and end at the same deck fitting. The tool's circles all sit on a sail edge, the rail or that fitting, so no rope ends in the air. The two mainsail sheets meet the bottom edge of the sail partway along rather than at its corners, which is an acceptable simplification. Railing posts stand on the deck. The ship has no bowsprit and simplified rigging, which counts as simplification. Everything attaches, the counts are consistent (3 masts, 3 yards, 3 sails, 3 flags), and the ship could sail.
